topics.title: What is Feature-Sliced Design and what problem does it solve?
topics.html:
FSD is a structural convention for frontend projects: layers → slices → segments, plus one hard rule about the direction of imports.

app/ providers, router, global styles, entry point pages/ route-level compositions (screens) widgets/ self-contained UI blocks (Header, OrderList panel) features/ user actions with business value (add-to-cart, login-form) entities/ business nouns + their model and UI (user, order, product) shared/ ui-kit, api client, lib, config — zero business logic slice = folder inside a layer → entities/user, features/login segment = ui | model | api | lib | config inside a slice
  • Import rule (the whole point): a module imports only from layers strictly below it. features may use entities and shared; entities must never import features. Slices on the same layer don't import each other.
  • Public API: every slice exposes an index.ts. Deep imports into internals are forbidden — that's what makes a slice refactorable without touching callers.
  • Enforcement is mechanical: ESLint boundaries rules or Steiger. An architecture nobody can violate by accident is the only kind that survives a year.
  • Payoff: deleting a feature means deleting a folder. Onboarding is "find the slice", not "grep the repo".
  • Cost: heavy ceremony on small apps; the entities/features boundary is genuinely ambiguous at the edges; cross-slice needs an explicit escape hatch.
💬 Say it like this

Feature-Sliced Design organises code by business meaning instead of by file type. Instead of one components folder with two hundred files, you have layers — shared, entities, features, widgets, pages — and a layer can only import from the layers below it. So all dependencies point in one direction, and you can see the coupling in the folder structure.

The part I like most is the public API rule: each slice exports through one index file, so I can rewrite everything inside it without breaking other code. And I check the import rule with an ESLint plugin, because a rule that nobody checks is forgotten after a few sprints.

When would you NOT use FSD?
Small app, small team, short lifetime — the ceremony costs more than the coupling it prevents. Also a bad fit if the team won't enforce it in CI: half-applied FSD is worse than plain feature folders.
Two features need each other. What do you do?
Usually a sign the shared part belongs one layer down (in an entity or in shared), or that the composition belongs one layer up (a widget/page wires both). FSD has explicit cross-import notation for the rare real case.
Where do shared types go?
Entity-owned types live in the entity's model segment and are re-exported from its index. Only truly generic types (Result, Nullable, ApiError) go to shared.

topics.title: Clean Architecture on the frontend — what does it actually mean?
topics.html:
One rule: dependencies point inward. Business rules never import the framework; the framework imports the business rules.

entities / domain pure TS: types, invariants, calculations ← knows nothing use cases application logic: "checkout", "applyDiscount" adapters api clients, mappers, storage, react-query hooks frameworks / UI React components, router, MUI React lives on the OUTSIDE. Domain code has no import from "react".
// domain — pure, testable without React, without a browser
export type Cart = { items: Item[]; currency: Currency };
export const cartTotal = (c: Cart): Money =>
  c.items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0);

// use case — depends on an interface, not on axios
export const checkout =
  (deps: { payments: PaymentsPort; cartRepo: CartRepo }) =>
  async (cartId: string) => {
    const cart = await deps.cartRepo.byId(cartId);
    if (cart.items.length === 0) throw new EmptyCartError();
    return deps.payments.charge(cartTotal(cart));
  };

// UI — thin: reads state, calls the use case, renders
function CheckoutButton({ cartId }: { cartId: string }) {
  const { mutate, isPending } = useMutation({ mutationFn: checkout(deps) });
  return <Button loading={isPending} onClick={() => mutate(cartId)}>Pay</Button>;
}
  • What you gain: business rules unit-testable with plain Vitest — no render, no mocks of fetch. Swapping REST for GraphQL, or React for React Native, touches only the outer ring.
  • What it costs: mapping layers and indirection. On a CRUD dashboard it's pure overhead — be honest about that in the interview, it reads as senior judgement.
  • Realistic version: most teams take one idea from it — keep calculations and rules in pure functions outside components — and skip the four-ring diagram.
💬 Say it like this

The main idea is the dependency rule: the inner layers — the domain and the use cases — know nothing about React, axios or the router. The outer layers depend on the inner ones, never the other way around. In practice my business logic is plain TypeScript functions that are fast and easy to test, and the component only calls them.

I don't use the full version on every project. On a normal dashboard it is too much. I keep the one rule that always helps: no business calculations inside components.

Does Clean Architecture conflict with FSD?
No — they answer different questions. FSD says where files live horizontally (which slice); Clean says which direction dependencies flow vertically. Many teams use FSD folders with a pure model segment inside each slice, which is Clean in miniature.
Where does React Query fit?
It's an adapter — infrastructure. The query function calls a repository interface; the domain doesn't know a cache exists.

topics.title: Hexagonal architecture (Ports & Adapters) — explain it in frontend terms.
topics.html:
A port is an interface the application owns. An adapter is a concrete implementation of it. The app talks to ports only, so any adapter can be swapped — real API, mock, localStorage, WebSocket.

// PORT — owned by the app, describes what it needs
export interface PaymentsPort {
  charge(amount: Money): Promise<Receipt>;
}

// ADAPTER 1 — production
export const httpPayments = (http: HttpClient): PaymentsPort => ({
  charge: (amount) => http.post("/payments", { amount }).then(toReceipt),
});

// ADAPTER 2 — tests / Storybook, no network at all
export const fakePayments = (): PaymentsPort => ({
  charge: async (amount) => ({ id: "test", amount, status: "paid" }),
});

// Injection point — one place decides which adapter is real
const Deps = createContext<{ payments: PaymentsPort }>(null!);
<Deps value={{ payments: import.meta.env.DEV ? fakePayments() : httpPayments(http) }}>
  • This is Dependency Inversion made concrete — the same "D" from SOLID, at module scale instead of component scale.
  • Frontend cases where it earns its keep: several backends behind one UI, a feature that must work offline, contract-unstable APIs, or a web + React Native shared core.
  • The lightweight React version is just passing fetchFn / a client object as a prop or through context instead of importing axios inside the component.
💬 Say it like this

Hexagonal means the application defines interfaces for everything it needs from the outside world, and the concrete implementations plug into those interfaces. So my checkout logic depends on a PaymentsPort, not on axios. In production I plug in the HTTP adapter; in tests and Storybook I plug in a fake one, and no test ever needs to mock the network.

Isn't that just dependency injection?
Yes — DI is the mechanism, hexagonal is the discipline of applying it at every boundary between the app and the outside world, with the interface owned by the app rather than by the vendor.

topics.title: FSD vs Clean vs Hexagonal vs Atomic Design — which solves what?
topics.html:
ApproachProblem it solvesUnit of thinkingUse it when
Feature-Sliced DesignWhere does this file go, and who may import itLayer / sliceLarge app, several teams, long lifetime
Clean ArchitectureBusiness rules leaking into UI and frameworkDependency directionReal domain logic, multi-platform core
HexagonalCoupling to concrete infrastructurePort / adapterSwappable or unstable external systems
Atomic DesignNaming and granularity of UI componentsAtom → organismDesign system / UI kit only
Feature foldersBasic co-location, nothing moreFolderSmall app, one team — the honest default
💬 Say it like this

They are not competitors, they answer different questions. FSD says where a file lives and what it can import. Clean says which way dependencies point. Hexagonal says how to isolate anything external. Atomic Design is only about the size of UI components in a library. On a real project I would use FSD folders, keep the model part pure like Clean says, and use ports for the API layer — and on a small app I would skip all of them.

topics.title: You join a 3-year-old React project with no architecture. How do you migrate to FSD without stopping delivery?
topics.html:
1. Measure first. Run madge --circular and a dependency graph. Name the three worst coupling clusters — you now have an argument, not an opinion.
  2. Create the layers empty and move only shared first: ui-kit, api client, utils. Lowest risk, immediate benefit, no business logic touched.
  3. Turn on the linter in warn mode (boundaries rules). Nothing breaks, but every new violation is visible in review.
  4. Migrate by touch, not by sprint. Whatever feature you're already working on gets moved into a slice as part of that ticket. No big-bang refactor branch — it will never merge.
  5. Extract entities as they repeat. When the third feature imports the same user-shaped type and mapper, that's an entity, not a guess.
  6. Flip the linter to error per layer as it becomes clean, so migrated ground can't regress.
  7. Write it down. One page in the repo: layers, import rule, and three examples. Convention without documentation lasts one onboarding.
💬 Say it like this

I would not do a big rewrite in one branch — those branches usually stay open for months and then get dropped. I start with the safest layer, shared, and turn the lint rule on in warning mode so everyone sees the direction in code review. After that the migration goes together with normal feature work: if I am already changing the cart, the cart becomes a proper slice in the same pull request. It is slower on paper, but it actually gets finished.

How do you sell this to a product manager?
In their currency: onboarding time, regression rate, "why does a small change take three days". Not "the architecture is bad".

topics.title: How do you enforce module boundaries in practice? Monorepo questions.
topics.html:
• Lint: eslint-plugin-boundaries or import/no-restricted-paths — declare layers, forbid upward and sideways imports. Steiger for FSD specifically.
  • Public API: forbid deep imports (features/*/ui/*) so slices stay refactorable. In packages, use the exports field in package.json — it's enforced by the resolver, not by convention.
  • Cycles: madge --circular in CI. Circular imports are the main cause of "undefined is not a function" at module init.
  • Monorepo: pnpm workspaces + Turborepo for task graph and caching; Changesets for versioning and changelogs of published packages.
  • Versioning a shared UI kit: semver strictly, breaking changes get a codemod and a deprecation release first, never a silent rename.
  • Ownership: CODEOWNERS per package, so boundary violations have an actual reviewer.
💬 Say it like this

An architecture that only exists in a wiki page does not survive. I make it automatic: ESLint rules for the import direction, the exports field so deep imports do not even work, and a check for circular dependencies in CI. Then the rule stops a pull request, and nobody has to police it by hand.
